name: Element of
definition: States that an object belongs to a set. x ∈ A means x is one of the members of A.

examples.explanation: Three is a member of the set containing 1, 2 and 3.

name: Not an element of
definition: States that an object is not a member of a set. It negates ∈.
reading: “x is not an element of A”.

examples.explanation: Four is absent from the set.

name: Proper subset
definition: States that every member of one set is a member of another, and the two sets differ. Convention varies: some authors let ⊂ include equality, so check the local definition.
reading: “A is a proper subset of B”.

examples.explanation: Both members sit inside the larger set, which has more.

commonMistakes: Assuming ⊂ always excludes equality; some texts use it for ⊆.

name: Subset or equal
definition: States that every member of one set lies in another, allowing the sets to be equal. Every set is a subset of itself under ⊆.

examples.explanation: A set is always a subset of itself.

name: Proper superset
definition: The mirror of proper subset: A ⊃ B means A contains everything in B and strictly more.
reading: “A is a proper superset of B”.

examples.explanation: The larger set contains the smaller and more.

name: Superset or equal
definition: The mirror of ⊆: every member of the right set lies in the left set, with equality allowed.

examples.explanation: Every rational number is real.

name: Union
definition: Collects everything in either set. An element belongs to A ∪ B when it belongs to A, to B, or to both.

examples.explanation: Shared members appear once; sets have no duplicates.

name: Intersection
definition: Keeps only what the sets share. An element belongs to A ∩ B when it belongs to both A and B.

examples.explanation: Only 2 sits in both sets.

name: Set difference
definition: Keeps the members of A that are absent from B. Unlike subtraction of numbers, order matters: A ∖ B usually differs from B ∖ A.

examples.explanation: Remove 2 from the set.

name: Set complement
definition: Collects everything outside A but inside the understood universal set. The complement depends on that universe, which must be clear from context.

examples.explanation: Within the universe U, the complement of {1} is {2, 3}.

name: Empty set
definition: The unique set with no members. It is a subset of every set, and it differs from zero, from nothing, and from a set containing the empty set.

examples.explanation: Nothing is both inside and outside A.

commonMistakes: Writing {∅} for the empty set; that is a set containing one member.

name: Power set
definition: The set of all subsets of A. A set with n members has 2ⁿ subsets, including the empty set and itself.

examples.explanation: All four subsets of a two-element set.

name: Set-builder notation
definition: Defines a set by a rule instead of listing members: the set of all x satisfying the stated condition. The bar (or a colon) reads as “such that”.
reading: “the set of all x such that…”.

examples.explanation: All positive numbers, without listing them.

name: Universal quantifier
definition: States that something holds for every member of a set. A single counterexample defeats a for-all claim.

examples.explanation: Every real number has a nonnegative square.

name: Existential quantifier
definition: States that at least one member of a set has a property. One example proves an existence claim.

examples.explanation: Some natural number exceeds 100; 101 will do.

name: Logical negation
definition: Flips a statement's truth value: ¬P is true exactly when P is false. Negating a quantified statement swaps for-all with there-exists.

examples.explanation: Denying “x is positive” leaves zero or negative.

name: Logical conjunction (and)
definition: Joins two statements so the combination holds only when both hold. P ∧ Q is true exactly when P and Q are each true.

examples.explanation: x is both positive and below 5: strictly between.

name: Logical disjunction (or)
definition: Joins two statements so the combination holds when at least one holds. Mathematical “or” is inclusive: both may hold.

examples.explanation: x is 0 or x is 1. Mathematical or is inclusive: both sides may hold, though here they cannot both hold at once.

commonMistakes: Reading or as exclusive; mathematics allows both sides true.

name: Implication
definition: States that whenever the left side holds, the right side follows. P ⇒ Q is falsified only by P true with Q false.
reading: “P implies Q” or “if P then Q”.

examples.explanation: Anything above 5 is automatically above 0.

commonMistakes: Assuming the converse: Q ⇒ P does not follow from P ⇒ Q.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Logical equivalence (if and only if)
definition: States that two statements imply each other: each holds exactly when the other does. Proving ⇔ needs both directions.

examples.tex: n \text{ is even } \Leftrightarrow n^2 \text{ is even}
examples.explanation: Each direction holds: even input, even square, and conversely.

name: Therefore
definition: Marks a conclusion drawn from preceding statements. It signals the result step of an argument, not a new assumption.

examples.explanation: The sum follows from the two values.

name: Because
definition: Marks a reason supporting a claim: the statement after ∵ justifies what came before. It is the mirror of ∴.

examples.explanation: The values justify the sum.

name: Cardinality
definition: Counts the members of a finite set. For infinite sets, cardinality compares sizes: two sets share a cardinality when their members can be paired one-to-one.
reading: “the cardinality of A” or “the size of A”.

examples.explanation: The set has three members.
Naturals and rationals pair off one-to-one.

name: End of proof (QED)
definition: Marks the end of a proof. Placed after the final line, it tells the reader the argument is complete; QED abbreviates the Latin “quod erat demonstrandum”.
reading: “Q E D” or “which was to be shown”.

examples.explanation: The proof ends with its concluding line marked.

name: Predicate
definition: A statement with a free variable that becomes true or false once x is specified. Predicates are what quantifiers ∀ and ∃ range over.

examples.explanation: P(7) is true; P(2) is false.
